title: How the Web Works: From URL to Rendered Page

questions.question: When you enter an unfamiliar URL and press Enter, what is the browser's first networking step?
options: Sending the HTTP request straight to the server
A DNS lookup to resolve the hostname into an IP address
Opening a TLS session for encryption
Downloading the page's CSS files
questions.rationale: No request can be routed until the hostname becomes an IP address, so after checking local caches the browser always performs a DNS lookup first.

questions.question: A DNS record has a TTL of 3600. What does that number control?
options: How long the TLS certificate stays valid
The TCP handshake timeout
How long the server keeps an idle connection open
How long the record may be cached before it must be re-queried
questions.rationale: TTL (time to live) states the seconds a resolver or browser may reuse the cached answer, which is why DNS changes propagate only as old TTLs expire.

questions.question: What is the correct order of the TCP three-way handshake?
options: SYN-ACK, SYN, ACK
ACK, SYN, SYN-ACK
SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
SYN, ACK, SYN-ACK
questions.rationale: The client sends SYN, the server answers SYN-ACK, and the client confirms with ACK, establishing ordered reliable delivery.

questions.question: What does TLS add on top of the raw TCP connection?
options: Server identity via certificates plus encryption of the channel
Faster packet routing between networks
Guaranteed ordering of packets
Compression of all HTTP headers
questions.rationale: TCP already provides ordering and reliability; TLS layers identity verification (certificates signed by authorities) and encryption on top, producing HTTPS.

questions.question: What is the difference between status codes 401 and 403?
options: 401 means forbidden forever; 403 means retry later
401 is a server error; 403 is a client error
401 means you are not authenticated (who are you?); 403 means authenticated but not allowed
They are interchangeable aliases for the same error
questions.rationale: 401 Unauthorized asks for credentials (log in first), while 403 Forbidden says identity is known but permission is denied.

questions.question: Which redirect status tells clients to update stored links and passes bookmarks and SEO weight onward?
options: 302 Found
304 Not Modified
301 Moved Permanently
307 Temporary Redirect
questions.rationale: 301 signals a permanent move, so clients and search engines transfer ranking and stored links to the new URL; 302 and 307 are temporary.

questions.question: What does the Cache-Control directive no-cache actually mean?
options: Never store the response anywhere
Store the response, but revalidate with the server before each use
Cache only in the browser, not in CDNs
Download every resource twice for safety
questions.rationale: no-cache is about validation, not storage: the copy may be kept but must be checked (e.g. with ETag) before reuse; no-store is the directive that forbids storage.

questions.question: A browser sends If-None-Match with ETag "v41" and the content has not changed. What does the server return?
options: 200 OK with the full body again
404 Not Found
412 Precondition Failed
304 Not Modified with the body omitted
questions.rationale: A matching ETag lets the server answer with the tiny 304 Not Modified response, saving the download while confirming the cached copy is current.

questions.question: The browser's render tree is built by combining which two structures?
options: The DOM tree and the CSSOM tree
The TCP session and the TLS session
The HTML source and the JavaScript heap
The cache manifest and the HTTP headers
questions.rationale: Parsing HTML builds the DOM, parsing CSS builds the CSSOM, and the render tree joins visible DOM nodes with their computed styles before layout and paint.

questions.question: Which statement captures the SEO trade-off between client-side and server-side rendering?
options: CSR is always better for SEO because crawlers execute all JavaScript
SEO depends only on the status codes the server returns
SSR delivers finished, crawlable HTML, while CSR builds content in the browser and needs extra work for crawlers
SSG has the worst SEO of the three approaches
questions.rationale: SSR and SSG send complete HTML that crawlers read directly; CSR ships a shell and relies on JavaScript to fill in content, which complicates indexing.
